sections.title: Greetings and farewells
sections.objective: Open, maintain briefly, and close a simple interaction appropriately.
sections.explanation: Recall complete chunks; choose informal tú or polite usted according to the situation.

patterns.form: Hola / Buenos días / Buenas tardes / Buenas noches
patterns.meaning: Hello / Good morning / Good afternoon / Good evening
How are things? — Fine, thanks. And you?

notes: Buenos días is normally used until lunch; buenas tardes afterwards.

examples.en: Hi, Ana. How are things?
Very well, thank you. And you?
Pleased to meet you.
See you on Monday.

commonMistakes.explanation: Día is masculine.
Cómo eres asks what someone is like.

practicePrompts.prompt: Greet a friend, ask how they are, and say goodbye.
Make “¿Cómo estás?” formal.
Give three different farewells.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: For example: adiós, hasta luego, hasta mañana.

checkpoints: I can greet someone formally and informally.
I can close a short conversation naturally.

sections.title: Personal information and introductions
sections.objective: Ask for and give basic information about identity, origin, residence, languages and contact details.
sections.explanation: Build a short self-introduction from memorised frames, then answer predictable follow-up questions.

patterns.meaning: I am from… but I live in…
Where are you from? / Where do you live?

patterns.form: ¿Cuál es tu número de teléfono/correo electrónico?

reference.answerFrame: Me llamo __. Soy de __. Vivo en __. Trabajo en __. Hablo __.

examples.es: Me llamo Alex y soy de Inglaterra.
examples.en: My name is Alex and I am from England.
I live near Manchester.

examples.es: Hablo inglés y un poco de español.
examples.en: I speak English and a little Spanish.
What do you do?

commonMistakes.incorrect: Soy de Manchester but vivo Manchester.
commonMistakes.explanation: Vivir needs en before a place.
Llamarse uses the reflexive pronoun me.

practicePrompts.prompt: Introduce yourself in five sentences.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Include name, origin, home, work/study and languages.

practicePrompts.prompt: Ask another learner four personal-information questions.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Use cómo, de dónde, dónde and qué.

practicePrompts.prompt: Spell an email address aloud, including arroba and punto.

checkpoints: I can give a 30-second introduction without notes.
I can understand and answer five common personal questions.

sections.title: Numbers, alphabet, spelling, dates and time
sections.objective: Recognise and produce numbers, spell words, and exchange dates, times, prices and phone numbers.
sections.explanation: Numbers are easy to recognise on paper but need aloud retrieval practice. Spanish letter names also support repair in conversation.

patterns.meaning: How is it spelt? — It is spelt…

patterns.form: ¿Qué hora es? — Es la una / Son las dos.
patterns.meaning: What time is it? — It is one / two.
How much is it? — It costs… euros.

reference.datePattern: Hoy es el veinte de septiembre.

examples.es: Mi número es el seis, uno, dos, cero, cuatro…
examples.en: My number is six, one, two, zero, four…

examples.es: La clase empieza a las diez y media.
examples.en: The class starts at half past ten.
It costs thirty-five euros.
Can you spell your surname?

commonMistakes.explanation: 21–29 are normally written as one word.
Use es only with one o’clock; son with other hours.

practicePrompts.prompt: Say 17, 24, 38, 76 and 101 aloud.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: diecisiete, veinticuatro, treinta y ocho, setenta y seis, ciento uno

practicePrompts.prompt: Say today’s date and three appointment times.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Use el + number + de + month; a la/las for times.

practicePrompts.prompt: Exchange and spell a surname, email address and telephone number.

checkpoints: I can understand prices and times at normal careful speed.
I can spell my name and email address.

sections.title: Gender, number and adjective agreement
sections.objective: Make common nouns, articles and adjectives agree in gender and number.
sections.explanation: Agreement usually follows the noun: many -o forms change to -a, and plurals add -s or -es. Learn exceptions with their article.

patterns.form: un chico alto / una chica alta
patterns.meaning: a tall boy / a tall girl

patterns.form: una ciudad grande / dos ciudades grandes
patterns.meaning: a big city / two big cities

examples.es: Es una ciudad pequeña y tranquila.
examples.en: It is a small, quiet city.
They are two young men.
The white houses are pretty.
I have an important problem.

commonMistakes.explanation: Problema is masculine.
Both noun and adjective must be plural.

practicePrompts.prompt: Make “un restaurante pequeño” feminine and plural.
Correct: “las chico españoles”.
Describe three objects around you using noun + two adjectives.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Check gender and number on every word.

checkpoints: I can form regular noun and adjective plurals.
I usually match articles and adjectives to the noun.

sections.title: Articles and demonstratives
sections.objective: Select definite/indefinite articles and identify nearby things with demonstratives.
sections.explanation: Articles agree with the noun. Use a definite article for a known or general class, and an indefinite article to introduce a non-specific item.

examples.en: I want a bottle of water.

examples.es: La botella está en la mesa.
examples.en: The bottle is on the table.
How much is this shirt?
I am going to the supermarket.

commonMistakes.explanation: Casa is feminine.
A + el contracts to al.

practicePrompts.prompt: Choose the correct form: __ libros (this/these).
Change “una camisa” to definite plural.
Point out four nearby objects using este/esta/estos/estas.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Match each demonstrative to its noun.

checkpoints: I can use all four definite and indefinite article forms.
I can use este-series demonstratives with agreement.

sections.title: Present tense: regular -ar, -er and -ir verbs
sections.objective: Form and use regular present-tense verbs in everyday statements and questions.
sections.explanation: Remove -ar, -er or -ir and add the ending for the subject. Spanish often omits subject pronouns because the verb ending identifies the person.

examples.en: I work in technology.
Where do you live?
We learn Spanish in class.

examples.es: Los domingos comemos con la familia.
examples.en: On Sundays we eat with the family.

commonMistakes.explanation: Use a conjugated verb, not the infinitive.
Use the nosotros ending -imos.

practicePrompts.prompt: Conjugate hablar, comer and vivir aloud in all six persons.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Use the reference table, then repeat from memory.

practicePrompts.prompt: Make six true sentences about your week using six regular verbs.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Vary the subject and verb group.

practicePrompts.prompt: Turn “Trabajas en Madrid” into a question and answer it.

checkpoints: I can retrieve regular endings without a table.
I can produce short present-tense sentences without always saying the subject pronoun.

sections.title: Essential irregular verbs
sections.objective: Use the most frequent irregular present-tense verbs as ready-to-speak forms.
sections.explanation: Prioritise high-frequency first-person forms and complete chunks rather than trying to infer every irregularity.

patterns.form: tengo / voy / hago / quiero / puedo / vengo / digo / sé / conozco

examples.en: I have to work this afternoon.
We are going to eat out.
Can you repeat, please?
I do not know this area.

commonMistakes.explanation: Saber has the irregular first person sé.
Poder takes the infinitive directly, without a.

practicePrompts.prompt: Say the yo form of all nine verbs.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: tengo, voy, hago, quiero, puedo, vengo, digo, sé, conozco

practicePrompts.prompt: Make one true sentence with ir a, tener que and poder.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Use a conjugated first verb plus an infinitive.

practicePrompts.prompt: Explain “sé” versus “conozco” using examples.

checkpoints: I can use the main yo forms immediately.
I can use ir a, tener que and poder with an infinitive.

sections.title: Ser and estar
sections.objective: Choose ser or estar for basic identity, description, condition and location.
sections.explanation: Use ser for identity, origin, profession, defining characteristics and time; estar for location and current condition.

reference.note: Do not reduce the contrast to permanent versus temporary; use the functional categories.

examples.en: I am British and I am a programmer.
I am tired but I am fine.
Valencia is in Spain.

examples.es: La reunión es a las tres.
examples.en: The meeting is at three.

commonMistakes.explanation: Location uses estar.
Profession uses ser, normally without an article.

practicePrompts.prompt: Choose ser or estar for origin, location, profession and mood.
Give two true sentences with ser and two with estar.
Correct: “La clase está a las diez.”
practicePrompts.answerGuide: La clase es a las diez.

checkpoints: I can give the present forms of ser and estar.
I can select the right verb in the main A1 situations.

sections.title: Questions and interrogatives
sections.objective: Ask and answer common information and yes/no questions with natural intonation.
sections.explanation: Spanish usually keeps statement word order and uses question marks and rising intonation; interrogative words carry written accents.

reference.punctuation: Use both opening ¿ and closing ? marks.
reference.personalA: ¿A quién…? when a person is the direct object.

examples.en: Where do you work?
What do you do at weekends?
How much does this jacket cost?

examples.es: ¿Por qué estudias español? Porque quiero trabajar en España.
examples.en: Why do you study Spanish? Because I want to work in Spain.

commonMistakes.explanation: The question phrase is two words and accented.
Use the accent and both question marks.

practicePrompts.prompt: Ask eight questions about a new classmate using eight interrogatives.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Keep the verb in the present tense.

practicePrompts.prompt: Turn “Vives en Londres” into a yes/no and an information question.
Answer “¿Por qué estudias español?” in two ways.

checkpoints: I can recall the main question words with accents.
I can ask follow-up questions without translating full English syntax.

sections.title: Intentions, wants and interests
sections.objective: Express plans, wants, needs and interests, and distinguish wanting from liking.
sections.explanation: Use conjugated modal-like verbs plus an infinitive. Treat me interesa/me gusta and polite ordering chunks as whole patterns.

patterns.form: Me interesa + singular/topic; me interesan + plural

contrasts.difference: general liking versus wanting one now

examples.en: I want to improve my Spanish.
I am going to work in Spain.
I am interested in technology.
I would like to book a table.

commonMistakes.explanation: Querer takes the infinitive directly.
The verb agrees with the thing that is interesting.

practicePrompts.prompt: Say that you like coffee, then order one.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Me gusta el café. Me gustaría/Quiero un café.

practicePrompts.prompt: State one plan, one need, one want and one interest.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Use voy a, necesito, quiero and me interesa.

practicePrompts.prompt: Politely request a table and two drinks.

checkpoints: I can distinguish quiero, me gusta and me gustaría.
I can state an immediate want and a future plan.

sections.title: Jobs and nationalities
sections.objective: State and ask about occupations and nationality with correct agreement.
sections.explanation: Professions after ser normally have no article. Nationality adjectives are lower-case in Spanish and agree with the person.

patterns.form: Trabajo de + profession / Trabajo en + sector/place

examples.es: Soy empresario y trabajo en tecnología.
examples.en: I am a business owner and work in technology.
She is a doctor.
We are British.
What field do you work in?

commonMistakes.explanation: Omit the article when simply naming a profession.
Use lower case and feminine agreement.

practicePrompts.prompt: Describe your work in three simple sentences.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Use soy, trabajo en/de and one regular verb.

practicePrompts.prompt: Make “un profesor español” feminine and plural.
Ask and answer nationality and occupation questions.

checkpoints: I can say what I and other people do.
I can match common nationalities to gender and number.

sections.title: Describing places
sections.objective: Give a simple description of a home, area or destination.
sections.explanation: Combine hay for what exists with es/son for character and está/están for location. Add a small set of high-value adjectives.

examples.es: Mi barrio es tranquilo y bastante moderno.
examples.en: My neighbourhood is quiet and quite modern.

examples.es: Hay dos parques y muchos cafés.
examples.en: There are two parks and many cafés.

examples.es: La estación está cerca del centro.
examples.en: The station is near the centre.

examples.es: Es bonito, pero es muy turístico.
examples.en: It is pretty, but very touristy.

commonMistakes.explanation: Use hay to introduce existence.

commonMistakes.incorrect: La ciudad es en el norte.
commonMistakes.correct: La ciudad está en el norte.
commonMistakes.explanation: Geographical location uses estar.

practicePrompts.prompt: Describe your neighbourhood in five sentences.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Use hay, es and está at least once each.

practicePrompts.prompt: Compare two towns using pero, más and menos as supporting language.
List six place adjectives with opposites where possible.

checkpoints: I can describe a place for 30 seconds.
I can introduce facilities and locate them.

sections.title: Weather and seasons
sections.objective: Understand and give a simple weather report and talk about seasonal conditions.
sections.explanation: Weather uses several fixed patterns: hace + noun/adjective, hay + noun, está + adjective/gerund, and impersonal verbs.

examples.es: Hoy hace sol, pero hace frío.
examples.en: Today it is sunny but cold.
It rains a lot in Manchester.
Tomorrow it is cloudy.
In summer it is quite hot.

commonMistakes.explanation: General weather temperature uses hacer.
Rain normally uses llover.

practicePrompts.prompt: Describe today’s weather and your preferred season.
Choose hace, hay, está or llueve for four weather descriptions.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Match each collocation, not an English “is”.

practicePrompts.prompt: Listen to a short forecast and note temperature, rain and wind.

checkpoints: I can answer ¿Qué tiempo hace? naturally.
I recognise the main weather constructions.

sections.title: Shopping, prices and quantities
sections.objective: Ask for items, sizes, prices and payment options in a shop.
sections.explanation: Use polite chunks plus demonstratives and numbers. Object pronouns can remain recognition-only at this stage.

patterns.meaning: I want / would like / am looking for…

examples.en: I am looking for a blue shirt.
Do you have this jacket in another size?
I want half a kilo of tomatoes.

examples.es: Son cuarenta y nueve euros con noventa.
examples.en: They are €49.90.

commonMistakes.explanation: The verb agrees with the singular item.
Quantity expressions take de.

practicePrompts.prompt: Buy a shirt: ask for colour, size, price and card payment.
Order three market items in different quantities.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Use kilo, medio kilo, gramos or botella.

practicePrompts.prompt: Practise hearing five prices and repeating them.

checkpoints: I can complete a basic shop transaction.
I can understand and say common quantities and prices.

sections.title: Survival language and communication repair
sections.objective: Keep an interaction going when vocabulary or comprehension fails.
sections.explanation: These phrases are high-value tools, not admissions of failure. Memorise them as immediate responses.

patterns.meaning: I do not understand. / I do not know.
What does… mean? / How do you say… in Spanish?

examples.en: Sorry, I do not understand. Can you repeat?
How do you spell “apellido”?
What does “sobremesa” mean?
I speak a little Spanish.

commonMistakes.explanation: Use a polite question with strangers.

commonMistakes.incorrect: No comprendo nada and switching immediately
commonMistakes.correct: No entiendo. Más despacio, por favor.
commonMistakes.explanation: Use a targeted repair request.

practicePrompts.prompt: Say five repair phrases without looking.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Include repeat, slower, spell, meaning and “I don’t understand”.

practicePrompts.prompt: Handle a speaker giving a phone number too quickly.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Interrupt politely and ask them to repeat digit by digit.

practicePrompts.prompt: Describe an unknown object using es una cosa que…
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Use simple known words, gesture or category.

checkpoints: I can repair a misunderstanding in Spanish.
I can ask for meaning, spelling and slower repetition.

sections.title: Core vowels, consonants and Spanish sounds
sections.objective: Pronounce the five stable vowels and decode the principal letter-to-sound rules of es-ES.
sections.explanation: Spanish spelling is relatively regular. Keep vowels pure and short; focus on consonants whose sound changes by context.

patterns.form: c + e/i → /θ/ in standard central/northern es-ES; c + a/o/u → /k/
h is silent; j is strong /x/

esESRules.c_z: c before e/i and z commonly use the “th” sound /θ/; seseo is also valid in many regions
esESRules.g_j: ge/gi and j use a strong velar sound
esESRules.b_v: b and v generally represent the same phoneme
esESRules.qu: qu before e/i gives /k/ and u is silent

examples.en: house, coffee, cinema, five
cat, guitar, people
hello, now, hotel
Spain, tomorrow, boy

commonMistakes.incorrect: Pronouncing Spanish vowels as English diphthongs.
commonMistakes.correct: Keep each vowel steady and pure.
commonMistakes.explanation: Spanish vowels change less during articulation.
Written h has no sound in standard Spanish.

practicePrompts.prompt: Read the example word sets slowly, then at natural speed.
Sort words by hard/soft c and g sounds.
practicePrompts.answerGuide: Use the following letter to decide.

practicePrompts.prompt: Record a 30-second introduction and check vowels, h, j, c/z and ñ.

checkpoints: I consistently produce the five Spanish vowels.
I can predict the main sounds of c, g, j, h, qu, ñ, ll and y.
